dedication, consecration

ety.text: Originated 1350–1400 from Middle English dedicacioun, from Old French dedicacion (“consecration of a church or chapel”), from Latin dēdicātiō, equivalent to dēdicātus+-iōn.

senses.d: The act of dedicating or the state of being dedicated.
ex: work with dedication
Her dedication is admirable.

senses.d: A note addressed to a patron or friend, prefixed to a work of art as a token of respect, esteem, or affection.
ex: Her dedication for the book was only a cryptic "Once again, for T".

senses.d: The event, or the ceremony celebrating it, marking an official completion, opening, or beginning.
ex: Near-synonym: inauguration
The building's dedication is scheduled for next week.

senses.d: The deliberate or negligent surrender of all rights to property.
ex: the dedication of this right-of-way

ety.text: from Middle English dedicat(e) (“dedicated”, also used as the past participle of dedicaten), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. The nouns is derived through substantivization from Latin dēdicātus, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

senses.d: To set apart for a deity or for religious purposes; consecrate.
To set apart for a special use.
ex: dedicated their money to scientific research.

senses.d: To commit (oneself) to a particular course of thought or action.
ex: dedicated ourselves to starting our own business.

senses.d: To address or inscribe (a literary work, for example) to another as a mark of respect or affection.
To open (a building, for example) to public use.
To show to the public for the first time.
ex: dedicate a monument.
Dedicate to nothing temporal.
His life is dedicate to worthiness.

senses.d: One who dedicates themselves, or who is dedicated, to the service of some leader, religion, etc.
ex: Rowan Cortak stood with the rest of the dedicates.

ety.text: From Middle French déduction, from Latin deductio. Equivalent to deduct + -ion or deduce + -tion.

senses.d: That which is deducted; that which is subtracted or removed.
ex: Near-synonyms: extract, reduction; see also Thesaurus:decrement

senses.d: A sum that can be removed in tax calculations, usually from the taxable amount; something that is written off.
ex: standard deduction
You might want to donate the old junk and just take the deduction.

senses.d: A sum withheld from an employee's pay for the purpose of paying tax.
A conclusion; that which is deduced, concluded or figured out.
ex: He arrived at the deduction that the butler didn't do it.

senses.d: The ability or skill to deduce or figure out; the power of reason
ex: Through his powers of deduction, he realized that the plan would never work.
